ethical_notes: 1) Ming military intervention, perpetrator named: in 1410-1411 the Ming treasure-fleet forces of the Yongle Emperor under Admiral Zheng He invaded the kingdom's southwestern core, seized the capital area, and captured king Vira Alakesvara together with his family and retainers, deporting them to Nanjing. This was an armed foreign intervention and forced deportation of a sovereign, not a 'diplomatic escort'. Chinese sources (Ming Shilu, Galle inscription context) frame Alakesvara as the aggressor who 'insulted' the fleet and preyed on shipping; Sinhala tradition (Rajavaliya) frames the Chinese as acting by stratagem and deceit. The dispute is recorded here, not resolved. Some Chinese accounts also claim the Buddha's Tooth Relic was carried to China; Sinhala tradition denies this — disputed. 2) Jaffna suzerainty and its violent overthrow: the Arya Chakravarti kings of Jaffna imposed tribute collection over Gampola's western ports (Colombo, Negombo, Chilaw, Panadura) and highland districts (Matale, Dumbara) from the 1350s; the Alagakkonara magnates of Raigama expelled and — per Sinhala chronicle tradition (Nikaya Sangrahaya) — executed Jaffna tax collectors, then destroyed the Jaffna two-pronged invasion (land army defeated at Matale, naval force at Dematagoda and Panadura). Both the Jaffna extraction and the Sinhalese reprisal killings are stated plainly. 3) The Zheng He voyages are celebrated in modern Chinese historiography as peaceful diplomacy; the 1411 Ceylon episode is the clearest counter-example and is presented as a war (Ming-Kotte War) with a king deposed by foreign force. 4) Parakramabahu VI's 1412 accession is presented in Ming records as an installation sanctioned by the Yongle court, and in Sinhala tradition as an indigenous restoration — both versions documented.

name_variants.name: ගම්පොල රාජධානිය
name_variants.context: Modern Sinhala rendering ('Gampola rajadhaniya' = Gampola Kingdom); attested as the Sinhala Wikipedia article title and Wikidata Sinhala label (fetched 2026-07-04). Modern label for the medieval polity, not a 14th-century attested unit.

name_variants.name: ගම්පොළ
name_variants.context: Modern standard Sinhala spelling of the town/kingdom name with retroflex ළ; given as the Sinhala form in the English Wikipedia infoboxes for both the kingdom and the town. Spelling varies between ල and ළ across modern sources.

name_variants.name: Gaṅgāsiripura
name_variants.context: Contemporaneous 14th-century name attested in Gampola-period inscriptions and chronicles ('resplendent city on the river', from its position on the Mahaweli Ganga); the closest thing to the polity's own attested capital name.
name_variants.source: Gampola-period epigraphy (Lankatilaka inscriptions); Culavamsa; en/si Wikipedia

name_variants.name: ගංගා ශ්‍රී පුර
name_variants.context: Sinhala-script form of Gangasiripura as given on Sinhala Wikipedia (also ගඟ සිරි පුර).

name_variants.name: Kingdom of Gampola
name_variants.source: en.wikipedia.org; K.M. de Silva, A History of Sri Lanka (1981)

name_variants.name: 錫蘭山國 (Xīlánshān guó)
name_variants.context: Ming Chinese name ('Ceylon Mountain country') for the Sinhala kingdom in Ming Shilu records and the Zheng He voyage accounts (1405-1411). Refers to the island polity the Ming encountered — i.e. the Gampola/Raigama state of Vira Alakesvara — not the town of Gampola specifically.

territory_changes.region: Central highlands — Gampola/Gangasiripura on the Mahaweli
territory_changes.description: Bhuvanaikabahu IV of the Dambadeniya-Kurunegala dynastic line moved the royal capital from Kurunegala to Gampola (Gangasiripura), supported by minister Senalankadhikara — a peaceful dynastic capital shift within the 'drifting capitals' pattern, not a conquest. Sources vary between 1341 and 1344/45 for his consecration.

territory_changes.region: Dedigama and the southwestern lowlands (later Raigama)
territory_changes.description: The kingdom functioned as a divided/co-ruled polity: Parakramabahu V ruled from Dedigama (c. 1344-1359) while Bhuvanaikabahu IV sat at Gampola; from the 1370s effective power over the southwest lay with the Alagakkonara family based at Raigama, with the Gampola king increasingly nominal.

territory_changes.region: Western ports (Colombo, Negombo, Chilaw, Panadura) and highland districts (Matale, Dumbara)
territory_changes.description: The Arya Chakravarti rulers of the Jaffna kingdom extended tribute and tax collection over Gampola's western coastal ports and even highland districts; Vikramabahu III (r. 1357-1374) paid tribute. A forced loss of fiscal sovereignty to Jaffna, imposed from a position of military-naval strength — dating of its onset (1350s-1360s) is approximate.

territory_changes.region: Southwestern lowlands and Matale — end of Jaffna suzerainty
territory_changes.description: Nissanka Alagakkonara of Raigama, chief minister under Vikramabahu III, fortified Kotte (c. 1370s), expelled and per the Nikaya Sangrahaya tradition executed the Jaffna tax collectors, and the Gampola-Raigama forces destroyed the Arya Chakravarti's two-pronged invasion: the land army defeated at Matale, the seaborne force routed at Dematagoda and its ships destroyed at Panadura (dated c. 1391 under Bhuvanaikabahu V; some accounts place the first expulsions from 1369). Perpetrators on both sides named: Jaffna's armed tax extraction was answered with Sinhalese reprisal killings and open war.

Ming intervention (Ming-Kotte War, 1410-11): after Vira Alakesvara's hostile reception of the treasure fleet (first clash 1405-06; the fleet returned via Galle in 1409, where Zheng He's trilingual inscription — inscribed in Nanjing 15 Feb 1409, in Chinese, Tamil and Persian — was erected), Admiral Zheng He's forces (~2,000 troops) marched inland, defeated the royal army, seized the capital, and captured Vira Alakesvara, deporting him with his family to Nanjing. Perpetrator: Ming China under the Yongle Emperor. Chinese accounts blame Alakesvara's aggression; Sinhala tradition alleges Chinese deceit — dispute recorded, not resolved.

territory_changes.region: Whole kingdom — seat moves to Raigama, then Kotte
territory_changes.description: With Vira Alakesvara deported, Parakramabahu VI was consecrated at Raigama in 1412 (Ming sources present his installation as sanctioned by the Yongle court; Sinhala tradition presents an indigenous accession) and subsequently moved the royal seat to Sri Jayawardenapura Kotte, closing the Gampola period and opening the Kingdom of Kotte. Vira Alakesvara was later released and returned from China without regaining power.

sources.citation: Cūḷavaṃsa: Being the More Recent Part of the Mahāvaṃsa, trans. Wilhelm Geiger (with C. Mabel Rickmers), Pali Text Society / Colombo, 1929-1930 — chapters XC-XCI cover the Gampola kings.
Nikāya Saṅgrahaya of Devarakkhita Jayabāhu Dharmakīrti (c. 1386) — contemporary Sinhala chronicle of the Gampola period covering the kings and the rise of the Alagakkonara family.

G.P.V. Somaratne, The Political History of the Kingdom of Kotte, 1400-1521 (Colombo, 1975; based on his SOAS PhD thesis, 'Political History of the Kingdom of Kotte, c. A.D. 1400-1521', University of London, 1969) — covers the Gampola-Kotte transition and the Chinese invasion.
K.M. de Silva, A History of Sri Lanka (London: C. Hurst & Co.; Berkeley: University of California Press, 1981) — the 'drift to the south-west' chapters on Gampola, Raigama and the Alagakkonara.

Edward L. Dreyer, Zheng He: China and the Oceans in the Early Ming Dynasty, 1405-1433 (New York: Pearson Longman, 2007) — the 1411 Ceylon campaign and capture of Vira Alakesvara from the Chinese documentary record (Ming Shilu, Ma Huan).

S. Paranavitana, 'The Tamil Inscription on the Galle Trilingual Slab', Epigraphia Zeylanica, Vol. III (1928-1933); first noticed by E.W. Perera, Spolia Zeylanica (1912-13) — the Galle Trilingual Inscription (inscribed Nanjing, 15 February 1409; discovered Galle 1911; now National Museum, Colombo).

ethical_notes: Violence and colonial coercion are explicit in this record. (1) Kotte's unification of the island was military conquest: in 1450 prince Sapumal (Tamil: Cempaka Perumal), commander for Parakramabahu VI of Kotte, conquered the Tamil kingdom of Jaffna in the second of two invasions; King Kanakasooriya Cinkaiariyan was driven into exile in South India. Tamil historiography (Yalpana Vaipava Malai tradition) records this from the conquered side; Jaffna regained independence in 1467. (2) The 1521 Vijayaba Kollaya ('spoiling of Vijayabahu'): the king's three sons had their father Vijayabahu VII murdered by a hired assassin and partitioned the kingdom (Kotte/Sitawaka/Raigama). (3) Portugal is the colonial power that destroyed and absorbed this kingdom. Portuguese arrival 1505/06 (Lourenco de Almeida); King Bhuvanekabahu VII was shot dead by a Portuguese soldier at Kelaniya in 1551 (accident or assassination — disputed, not resolved here); his grandson Dharmapala was installed as a client king under Portuguese military tutelage, baptized Dom Joao in 1557, and lived under Portuguese protection in the Colombo fort after Kotte city was abandoned in 1565. His 1580 deed of donation bequeathing the kingdom to the Portuguese crown was a coerced client-state act by a ruler wholly dependent on Portuguese arms — NOT a free gift; it took effect at his death on 27 May 1597, creating Portuguese Ceylon. (4) The sister kingdom Sitawaka (1521-1594) mounted the fiercest armed resistance to Portugal; Portuguese forces sacked Sitawaka city in 1594 after Rajasinha I's death (1593). Portuguese campaigns in this period included destruction of Buddhist and Hindu temples, documented even in the pro-Portuguese Jesuit chronicle of Queiros. Disputes recorded, not resolved: 1505 vs 1506 arrival date; regnal chronology of Kotte kings c. 1467-1509; Kandy's secession dated 1469 by most sources (some argue early 1470s); nature of Bhuvanekabahu VII's death.

name_variants.name: කෝට්ටේ රාජධානිය
name_variants.context: Modern Sinhala historiographic name (Kotte Rajadhaniya, 'Kingdom of Kotte'); attested as native_name in Sinhala/English Wikipedia. The Sinhala script form is a modern rendering, not a 15th-century attestation.

name_variants.name: Sri Jayawardhanapura Kotte (ජයවර්ධන කෝට්ටේ)
name_variants.context: Contemporary name of the fortified capital and by extension the polity, attested in Kotte-era sources (Rajavaliya; 15th-c. Sandesha poetry such as Salalihini Sandeshaya); 'Jayawardhana' = 'victory-increasing', 'Kotte' from Malayalam/Tamil kottai = fort.

name_variants.name: Cota / Reino de Cota
name_variants.context: Portuguese colonial-era spelling, used in Portuguese sources including Queiros, Conquista Temporal e Espiritual de Ceylao.
name_variants.source: F. de Queiros, trans. S.G. Perera (1930)

territory_changes.description: Parakramabahu VI acceded in 1412 (initially at Raigama; capital moved to the fortress of Kotte c. 1415), founding the kingdom as successor to Gampola. His rise followed the 1411 Ming intervention in which admiral Zheng He's forces captured the previous strongman Vira Alakeshvara and took him to Nanjing — a non-Western (Chinese) dimension of the founding recorded in both the Rajavaliya and the Ming shi.

Prince Sapumal (Tamil: Cempaka Perumal), adopted son and commander of Parakramabahu VI, conquered the Tamil Jaffna kingdom in the second of two invasions (the first failed). King Kanakasooriya Cinkaiariyan fled to South India. With Jaffna, the Vanni chiefs and the hill country subdued, Kotte ruled the whole island — the last time a single Sri Lankan polity did so until 1815. Sapumal governed Jaffna 1450-1467.

Kanakasooriya Cinkaiariyan returned from Madurai with mercenary forces and retook Jaffna after Sapumal left north to contest the Kotte succession (he took the throne as Bhuvanekabahu VI). Jaffna's independence from Kotte was restored.
Senasammata Vikramabahu rebelled against Kotte and made the hill country (Kandy) independent — origin of the Kandyan kingdom. Most sources date this 1469; some historians argue the early 1470s.

First Portuguese arrival: Lourenco de Almeida's squadron, blown to the island's southwest coast (late 1505 or 1506 — date disputed), reached the Kotte court. Portugal extracted trade concessions, built a fort at Colombo in 1518, and began the armed intrusion that would consume the kingdom.

territory_changes.region: Kotte partitioned into Kotte, Sitawaka and Raigama
territory_changes.description: Vijayaba Kollaya ('spoiling of Vijayabahu'): the king's three sons — Bhuvanekabahu, Pararajasingha and Mayadunne — mutinied on learning their father intended to make his stepson Devaraja heir, and had King Vijayabahu VII murdered in his chamber by a hired assassin. They split the realm: Bhuvanekabahu VII kept Kotte and the seaboard, Mayadunne took Sitawaka (which became the fiercest anti-Portuguese resistance state, 1521-1594), Pararajasingha took Raigama.

King Bhuvanekabahu VII was shot dead by a Portuguese soldier at Kelaniya — accident or assassination, disputed to this day. Portugal installed his young grandson Dharmapala under Portuguese military tutelage; he was baptized Dom Joao in 1557, becoming a Catholic client king dependent on Portuguese arms against Sitawaka.

territory_changes.region: Capital: Kotte city abandoned for Colombo
territory_changes.description: Unable to withstand repeated Sitawaka assaults under Mayadunne and Rajasinha I, the Portuguese abandoned the city of Kotte; Dharmapala's court was moved inside Portuguese-held Colombo, completing his reduction to a protected puppet.

Dharmapala, a client king living under Portuguese protection in Colombo, executed a deed of donation bequeathing the whole kingdom of Kotte to the Portuguese crown on his death. A coerced client-state act under military tutelage, not a free gift: the perpetrator-beneficiary was colonial Portugal (from 1580 under the Habsburg Philip II as king of Portugal).

After Rajasinha I of Sitawaka died in 1593, Portuguese forces sacked the city of Sitawaka in 1594 and absorbed its lowland territories, ending the strongest indigenous resistance to Portuguese expansion; their same-year Danture campaign into Kandy was crushed by Vimaladharmasuriya I.

territory_changes.region: Entire Kotte kingdom to Portuguese Ceylon
territory_changes.description: Dharmapala died 27 May 1597 in the Colombo fort. Under the 1580 donation, colonial Portugal annexed the kingdom outright as Portuguese Ceylon — the formal end of Kotte. The absorption was the culmination of a half-century of coercion, client-kingship and war, not a voluntary transfer.

sources.citation: Somaratne, G.P.V. (1975). The Political History of the Kingdom of Kotte, 1400-1521. Nugegoda: Deepanee Printers. (Based on his SOAS PhD thesis, 'Political history of the Kingdom of Kotte, c. A.D. 1400-1521'.)

Queiros, Fernao de (c. 1687). The Temporal and Spiritual Conquest of Ceylon [Conquista Temporal e Espiritual de Ceylao]. Translated by S.G. Perera, 3 vols. Colombo: Government Printer, 1930. Jesuit chronicle; pro-Portuguese primary source, used critically.

Gunasekara, B., ed. and trans. (1900). The Rajavaliya: or, A Historical Narrative of Sinhalese Kings from Vijaya to Vimala Dharma Surya II. Colombo: Government Printer. Sinhala chronicle; primary source for the Vijayaba Kollaya and the Kotte period from the Sinhala side.

de Silva, K.M. (1981). A History of Sri Lanka. London: C. Hurst / Berkeley: University of California Press. Standard academic survey covering Kotte, the 1521 partition, Sitawaka resistance and the Portuguese absorption.
